common_name: Orange Energy Seaberry (Sea Buckthorn Fruiting Shrub)

planting.note: Plant one male seaberry for every six to eight females since the species is dioecious, and keep the planting site dry and sunny rather than humid to avoid fungal problems.

directions: Orange Energy is a sea buckthorn selection bred for exceptionally high vitamin C and E content in its tart orange berries, borne on thorny, silvery-leaved shrubs that thrive in poor, sandy soils. Being dioecious, it requires a separate male seaberry nearby for pollination, with one male typically sufficient to service six to eight female plants. It is notably drought-tolerant once established and does best in dry, full-sun climates like the Pacific Northwest or similar regions, since humid summers invite fungal disease. Because fruit forms on older wood, prune in summer to open up the canopy and keep the lower branches productive and harvestable.

planting.note: Plant very early since honeyberries flower before most fruiting shrubs, and site with a compatible pollinator such as Blue Velvet or Blue Pagoda, as this variety is not self-fertile.

directions: Blue Sea is a Northern Japanese honeyberry selection prized for producing unusually large, sweet blueberry-like fruit on a compact, cold-hardy shrub only 2 to 3 feet tall. It flowers quite late for a honeyberry and is not self-fertile, so it needs a compatible pollinator variety, such as Blue Velvet, Kamchatka, or Blue Pagoda, planted nearby to produce a crop. It tolerates a wider soil pH range than blueberries and appreciates organic-rich soil with roughly 5 to 10 percent organic matter. Give it full sun in cool-summer areas, but expect it to tolerate considerably more shade in hotter climates, and prune in summer to keep air moving through the spur-bearing branches.

common_name: Peking Alpine Bells (Primrose-Relative for Shaded Rock Gardens)

planting.note: Tuck divisions into a cool, moist pocket of a shaded rock garden or streamside bed where roots will not bake in summer.

directions: A diminutive relative of Primula, this plant forms a soft, downy clump of rounded, deeply cut leaves topped by wiry stems carrying nodding, bell-shaped rosy-purple flowers with pale centers. It comes from cool streamside woodlands in Japan and northern China, so it wants a consistently damp, shaded niche rather than a hot, dry one. Use it as a small-scale accent at the front of a shaded border or alongside a woodland path where its delicate umbels can be appreciated up close.

planting.note: Plant alongside Epimedium or other shade perennials in cool, humus-rich soil for a fragrant blue accent in the woodland border.

directions: Selected from a Sichuan collecting trip, this cultivar bears finely cut, blue-green ferny foliage and clusters of intensely saturated, fragrant sapphire-blue flowers in spring, among the deepest blue tones in the genus. It stays compact and well mannered, making it a good small-scale companion plant rather than a spreader. Give it cool, evenly moist, humus-rich soil in a lightly shaded spot and expect it to go semi-dormant if conditions turn hot and dry.

common_name: Black-Footed Wood Fern (Asian Fern for Damp Shade)

planting.note: Site near a pond edge or in a consistently damp, shaded border in compost-enriched soil.

directions: An upright, clump-forming Asian fern notable for the fuzzy black bases on its new croziers, which unfurl into glossy evergreen fronds up to two feet long. It is easy to grow once given a consistently damp, humus-rich spot and tolerates the darker reaches of a woodland garden better than many other ferns. Use it near water features or at the back of a shaded border for year-round structure, and avoid letting the root zone dry out.

common_name: Margery Fish Bleeding Heart (Smoky Blue-Leaved Fringed Bleeding Heart)

planting.note: Plant in cool, humus-rich soil in a shaded border and expect the foliage to go summer-dormant if the ground dries out.

directions: This fernleaf bleeding heart forms a low, soft mound of finely cut, smoky blue-gray foliage, with pale heart-shaped flowers marked by a small pink blush dangling from branched sprays in spring and again in fall. It is a good lacy filler for the front of a shaded border or a cottage-style woodland planting. Keep the soil cool, moist, and well drained through the growing season, but don't be alarmed if it dies back to the roots during a hot, dry spell.

common_name: Soryu Blue Dragon Ground Orchid (Cold-Hardy Terrestrial Orchid)

planting.note: Plant tuberous rhizomes in dappled shade with evenly moist, well-drained soil and apply a heavy winter mulch in colder zones.

directions: A genuinely cold-hardy terrestrial orchid, this seed-grown selection produces ribbed, iris-like foliage and slender stems of enchanting blue-violet, Cattleya-shaped blooms with pleated lips. The tuberous rhizomes slowly expand the clump year over year, making it a long-term investment rather than an instant filler. Give it dappled woodland shade, evenly moist but well-drained soil, and a thick winter mulch where temperatures dip hard, and it will tolerate occasional dry spells once established.
